notes:
Below are notes on Ephesians 4, verse by verse. I only had time to read part of what I planned, so some verses have more on them than others. What I couldn't find is listed at the end.

---

**v. 1: Prisoner, "therefore", walking worthy**
- **The reason for obeying.** Guzik says Paul gives this call to live rightly only after three chapters about what God has done. We don't walk worthy so that God will love us, but because He does love us. It is motivated out of gratitude, not out of a desire to earn merit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-4/
- **"Walk" means how you live.** NET: "walk" refers to the conduct of one's life. The "calling" is the Spirit's prompting that brought them to believe. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/eph4_notes.htm
- **Why Paul calls himself a prisoner.** Benson says Paul was imprisoned for the gospel's sake and theirs, which gave them a powerful motive to them to comfort him under his sufferings by their obedience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/4-1.htm
- **Two duties.** Matthew Henry says the chapter stresses unity and purity. In his view we don't walk worthy if we be not faithful friends to all Christians, and sworn enemies to all sin. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eph/Eph_004.cfm

**v. 2: Humility, gentleness, patience**
- **Humility and gentleness.** Guzik: a worthy walk is marked by these, not by a pushy desire to defend our own rights and advance our own agenda. He cites Chrysostom: patience (longsuffering) is the power to take revenge while never using it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-4/
- **Links to the Beatitudes.** Ellicott connects the three qualities to the first, third and fifth Beatitudes. He notes that the word for "lowliness" is a new Christian word; pagan moralists mostly used its root in a bad sense, meaning meanness or slavishness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ephesians/4.htm
- **"Gentleness."** NET notes the word was often used for the merciful execution of justice on behalf of those who have no voice by those who are in a position of authority. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/eph4_notes.htm
- **Bearing with one another.** Henry: bearing with others' weaknesses out of love, and not ceasing to love them because of those weaknesses. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eph/Eph_004.cfm

**v. 3: Keeping the unity of the Spirit**
- **We keep it; we don't make it.** We must endeavor to keep this unity – we do not create it. God never commands us to create unity among believers. He has created it by His Spirit; our duty is to recognize it and keep it. Guzik, drawing on Spurgeon, adds that a merely structural unity can work against true unity of the Spirit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-4/
- Ellicott agrees: the unity is God's gift, but keeping it takes real effort against evils inside and outside us. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ephesians/4.htm
- **The verb is strong.** The Pulpit Commentary says the Greek is stronger than "endeavouring" and describes something to be watched over and promoted with care. https://biblehub.com/ephesians/4-3.htm
- **Damaged, not destroyed.** Pulpit: people can't destroy this unity, though he can thwart or disturb its manifestations. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ephesians-4.html

**v. 4: One body, one Spirit, one hope**
- **An early creed.** Ellicott says "There is" isn't in the Greek. The verse opens abruptly, in a compressed style that marks out an embryo creed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/4-4.htm
- **Gill:** "one" body because Jews and Gentiles, saints in heaven and on earth, and separate congregations make up one church under one head. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/4-4.htm
- **Pulpit, with a Protestant edge.** The real body is not synonymous with any single outward society. It also says this church cannot be identified with the Roman Catholic Church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/4-4.htm

**v. 5: One Lord, one faith, one baptism (traditions differ here)**
- **Pentecostal-leaning (Guzik).** Some say "one baptism" rules out a later baptism of the Holy Spirit. Guzik replies that Paul only spoke here of the baptism by water which is the visible token of God's common work in every believer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-4/
- **Reformed (Ligonier).** The "one baptism" is the Spirit's baptism that joins us to Christ. It is related to water baptism, yet it is not identical to it, so water baptism should also happen only once. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/one-lord-one-faith-one-baptism
  - Ligonier also uses this verse against rebaptising someone baptised as an infant. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/one-baptism
- **Calvin:** baptism is shared by all, and since it is given in the name of the Three Persons, it points to one God in three. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/4-5.html
- **Gill** (believer's baptism by immersion). There is only one proper baptism, water baptism, to be given by immersion to believers in Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/4-5.htm
- **Barnes:** the verse is about baptism itself, not one method. Whether by immersion, pouring or sprinkling, as adults or infants, all have received the same act of consecration. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/4-5.htm
- **Coffman (Restoration Movement):** it is the baptism of the Great Commission, not Spirit baptism. He blames post-Reformation commentators for bias toward "faith only." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/4-5.html
- **Other commentators who say it means Spirit baptism, or both:**
  - Constable thinks both were probably in Paul's mind, leaning toward water. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/4-5.html
  - The Biblical Illustrator prefers Spirit baptism. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/4-5.html
  - GotQuestions says it could be either; either way the point is unity. https://www.gotquestions.org/one-baptism.html
- **Scholarly opinion.** A bible.org article says the scholarly consensus is that this refers to water baptism. https://bible.org/article/one-baptism-ephesians-45
- **Ellicott (Anglican-style):** baptism is the way into unity and can be given (though irregularly) by any Christian hand. Most of Christendom is still united in it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/4-5.html
- **Why baptism and not the Lord's Supper?** JFB, quoting Ellicott: baptism brings us into the body, while the Supper is "a symbol of union, not of unity". https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Eph/Eph_004.cfm

**v. 6: One God and Father**
- **Ellicott:**
  - The Father is "the fount of Deity."
  - His fatherhood can't be limited to Christians, though the context mainly means his adopted children.
  - Many see the Trinity in "over, through, in." Strictly, Ellicott says, all three refer to the Father.

  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ephesians/4.htm

**v. 7: Grace given to each**
- **Ellicott:** the one grace was given to the whole body but must be received by each person over time. Christ has it "without measure" and gives it to each according to their capacity to receive. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ephesians/4.htm
- **Henry:** different gifts should not lead to different levels of affection, since all come from the same giver. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eph/Eph_004.cfm
- **Guzik (French edition):** spiritual gifts rest on grace, so no one earns them. https://fr.enduringword.com/ephesiens-4/

**v. 8: Psalm 68 quoted**
- **Guzik:** the giving happened at Christ's ascension, as Psalm 68:18 foretold, and shows his triumph over every foe. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-4/
- **Ellicott:**
  - Psalm 68 celebrates moving the ark, probably David bringing it to Zion.
  - "Led captivity captive" is popularly read as Christ's victory over evil. Ellicott says that is true in itself, but the Greek simply means "a body of captives."

  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/4-8.htm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ephesians/4.htm
- **Modern scholarship (NET).** The Hebrew and Greek texts of Psalm 68 say "received gifts," not "gave gifts." NET lists three explanations:
  - Paul adapted the text, as rabbis sometimes did.
  - He quoted a version of the psalm that has since been lost.
  - He quoted an early Christian hymn.

  https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/eph4_notes.htm

**vv. 9–10: "Descended to the lower parts of the earth" (much debated)**
- **NET lists three views:**
  1. The traditional view: Christ went down to the underworld between his death and resurrection.
  2. "The lower parts, namely, the earth," meaning the incarnation. Many recent scholars hold this.
  3. The descent comes after the ascension and means the Spirit coming at Pentecost. Jewish writers read Psalm 68 as Moses going up Sinai, so Paul may be arguing against that reading.

  NET also notes that "first" ("descended first") was probably added by later copyists. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/eph4_notes.htm
- **Precept Austin:** descent into Hades was the view held by the early church fathers but which is less popular with modern evangelical commentators. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60174/
- **The incarnation reading:**
  - Calvin: the words mean only this present life, and making them mean purgatory or hell is "exceedingly foolish." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/4-9.html
  - Piper (Desiring God): it means Christ came down to earth, and the verse doesn't support a descent into hell. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/did-christ-ever-descend-to-hell
  - GotQuestions agrees, given the context. https://www.gotquestions.org/descended-into-the-lower-parts-of-the-earth.html
  - Barnes: Christ's lowest humiliation on earth. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/4-9.html
- **The grave:**
  - Pulpit: the Hades reading has no good reason; if more than humility is meant, it is the grave. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/4-9.html
  - Spurgeon: Christ went down into the tomb. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/4-9.html
  - Benson, citing Bishop Pearson: the text is weak proof for a descent into hell, because the phrase elsewhere means the womb or the grave. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/4-9.html
- **Gill:** probably the whole of Christ's humiliation. If "descent into hell" is meant, it is not a place but bearing God's wrath. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/4-9.htm
- **Hades / underworld:**
  - Meyer: Christ went below the earth into Hades. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/4-9.htm
  - Cambridge Bible: many Church Fathers saw a rescue of Old Testament saints here, but certainly the words here teach nothing of the kind. It says only that Christ entered the state of the dead. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/4-9.htm
  - Chuck Smith (Smith's Bible Commentary): Christ went to the part of Hades where the faithful dead were waiting, to lead them into glory. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/4-9.html
- **Catholic (Haydock):** the words can't mean only the grave, since the Creed confesses both "buried" and "descended into hell." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ephesians/4-9.html
- **v. 10, "fill all things":** Ellicott links it to Christ "filling all in all" (1:23). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ephesians/4.htm

**v. 11: Apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers (traditions differ)**
- **Christ's gift.** Ellicott: "He" is emphatic, and They who are ministers of His gifts are themselves gifts from Him to the Church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ephesians/4.htm
- **Four offices or five?**
  - Guzik: grammatically four, with pastor/teacher as one. He also says the verse doesn't mean every congregation needs its own apostle and prophet. https://enduringword.com/should-the-fivefold-ministry-be-restored/
  - NET: the plural nouns are unlikely to be one group. Pastors are a subset of teachers. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/eph4_notes.htm
- **Pentecostal (Assemblies of God position paper):**
  - Revelatory apostolic and prophetic roles belonged to the founding era.
  - Some apostolic and prophetic functions ought to be present in every generation.
  - The best word is "manifold," not fivefold or fourfold.

  https://ag.org/Beliefs/Position-Papers/Apostles-and-Prophets and https://ag.org/-/media/AGORG/Beliefs/Position-Papers/Apostles-and-Prophets.pdf
- **Pneuma Review:** restoring the "fivefold ministries" has stirred great interest in Pentecostal-charismatic circles. http://pneumareview.com/apostolic-practice/
- **Cessationist and Reformed:**
  - MacArthur (GTY): the apostolic office is a gift, and it has ceased, so charismatics can't say all the gifts continue. https://shop.gty.org/library/blog/B131218
  - Ligonier: apostles and prophets were the church's foundation, so they are no longer needed. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/gift-officers
  - Precept Austin agrees and rejects apostolic succession. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ephesians_411
- **The popular "restoration" teaching.** GotQuestions describes the claim that, since the church hasn't yet reached v. 13's maturity, apostles and prophets must still be active. It answers that the Bible already gives the church everything it needs. https://www.gotquestions.org/five-fold-ministry.html

**v. 12: Equipping the saints**
- **Guzik:** leaders equip God's people for service so the body is built up. In the chapter he contrasts the church with a pyramid with a pastor at the top or a bus driven by a passive congregation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-4/
- **The "comma" question.** Ellicott says the King James Version's three parallel phrases don't quite match the Greek, which uses one preposition for the first phrase and another for the last two. Chrysostom, though, read it the KJV way. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ephesians/4.htm
- **NET:** "to equip the saints" is the core; "works of ministry" explains it further. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/eph4_notes.htm
- **Assemblies of God:** the current focus on v. 11 neglects v. 12, which stresses that every believer ministers. https://ag.org/Beliefs/Position-Papers/Apostles-and-Prophets

**v. 13: Unity and maturity**
- **Ellicott:** the first aim of every ministry is that everyone fully grasps the "one faith." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ephesians/4.htm
- **Gill:** the gospel ministry continues until all God's elect come in. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/4-13.htm

**v. 14: No longer infants**
- **Guzik:** being steady comes through sound leaders and equipped saints. Mere movement is being "tossed to and fro," not growth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-4/
- **NET:** Paul fears cunning people teaching false doctrine that stunts believers' growth. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/eph4_notes.htm
- **JFB:** the various teachings are "winds" keeping people on a sea of doubt. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Eph/Eph_004.cfm

**v. 15: Speaking the truth in love**
- **Guzik:** deal with deceivers in love, but never move from the truth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-4/
- **Ellicott:** truth without love becomes hard and stoic; love without truth can become idolatry. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ephesians/4.htm
- **NET:** the verb probably means "being truthful" in both conduct and speech, not only speaking. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/eph4_notes.htm

**v. 16: The whole body growing**
- **Ellicott:** "fitted together" is a building word ("bonded together"). Each part working at its proper capacity is the condition for the whole body's growth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ephesians/4.htm
- **NET:** the word for "held together" can also suggest teaching. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/eph4_notes.htm

**vv. 17–19: The old way of life**
- **Guzik:** human ignorance is at root a heart problem, seen in moral failure. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-4/
- **Ellicott:** compare Romans 1:21–32. Losing God means losing the purpose of life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ephesians/4.htm
- **Henry:** God did make himself known, but they would not let the light in. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eph/Eph_004.cfm
- **NET on "craving for more":** sinful desires are never satisfied. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/eph4_notes.htm

**vv. 20–24: Put off the old self, put on the new**
- **Guzik:** they "learned Christ" himself, not just facts about him. Don't wait to feel new before putting on the new self. The new self is the new creation made at conversion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-4/
- **Command or fact? (NET).** "Put off… be renewed… put on" may be commands, or statements that "you have put off… you have put on." NET translates them as commands but calls the other reading plausible. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/eph4_notes.htm
- **Pulpit:** inward renewal should show in outward renovation. https://biblehub.com/ephesians/4-24.htm

**v. 25: Truthfulness**
- **NET:** a quotation from Zechariah 8:16. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/eph4_notes.htm
- **Ellicott:** vv. 25–30 deal with lying, anger, stealing and impurity, matching the Ninth, Sixth, Eighth and Seventh Commandments. Paul treats them in terms of unity in Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ephesians/4.htm

**vv. 26–27: "Be angry, yet do not sin"**
- **NET, citing Wallace:**
  - It is a command, not "if you are angry."
  - It calls for righteous indignation at sin within the church, confronted gently and quickly; otherwise the devil gains a foothold. Wallace calls it shorthand for church discipline.
  - "Anger" in v. 26b may mean the *cause* of anger.

  https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/eph4_notes.htm
- **Henry:** the danger is letting anger burn into wrath and settle. Some read "devil" as "false accuser," meaning: don't listen to slanderers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eph/Eph_004.cfm
- **Guzik:** harbouring anger does the devil's work by dividing God's family. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-4/

**v. 28: Stealing and work**
- **Guzik:** we work in order to give, a complete reversal of the world's purpose. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-4/
- **Henry:** even labourers must give to the poor, but charity must come from honest work, not robbery. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eph/Eph_004.cfm

**v. 29: Wholesome talk**
- **Henry:** foul talk is like rotten meat. Speech is meant to build up. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eph/Eph_004.cfm
- **NET:** "the need" may mean the need of the moment or the person's need. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/eph4_notes.htm

**v. 30: Grieving the Spirit; sealed**
- **Ellicott:** the verse covers all the commands before it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/4-30.htm
- **MacLaren:** the verse warns of a person's power and freedom to thwart the Spirit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/4-30.htm
- **Gill:** the Spirit's being grieved shows in his withdrawing, seen in darkness of soul and weak grace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ephesians/4-30.htm
- **Henry:** the Spirit is God's seal and guarantee of the resurrection. we should be undone should God take away his Holy Spirit from us. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eph/Eph_004.cfm
- **Spurgeon (via Guzik):** the Spirit is grieved when we love worldly things more than him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-4/

**v. 31: Getting rid of bitterness**
- **Henry:** bitterness, wrath and anger are inner resentment; clamour and slander are how they spill out in words. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eph/Eph_004.cfm
- **Guzik:** the new self controls these emotions and handles them in a way that honours God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ephesians-4/

**v. 32: Forgive as God forgave**
- **Henry:** forgive as God does, sincerely, readily and forever, upon the sinner's sincere repentance. He links this to the Lord's Prayer. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eph/Eph_004.cfm
- **Guzik (French edition):** God's forgiveness is the pattern. He makes the first move, gives no probation period, and bears the whole cost himself. https://fr.enduringword.com/ephesiens-4/

---

**What I couldn't find (left out):**
- Nothing from newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org. The only Catholic voice is Haydock on v. 9, via StudyLight.
- Nothing from the Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org) or the Wesleyan sites (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com).
- Nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter. The only debated popular teaching I found is the "fivefold ministry restoration" claim at v. 11.
- Nothing directly on whether v. 30's "sealed" supports eternal security.
